features.name: Cassini Division
features.description: The most famous gap in Saturn's rings, the Cassini Division is a 4,800-kilometre-wide region that appears nearly empty from Earth. It was discovered by Giovanni Cassini in 1675 and is carved by a 2:1 orbital resonance with the moon Mimas.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Though called a 'gap', the Cassini Division actually contains faint ringlets — it's not truly empty. The Huygens Gap is its darkest core.

features.name: Huygens Gap
features.description: The deepest and widest gap within the Cassini Division, the Huygens Gap marks the inner boundary of the division. It is named after the Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens, who first correctly described Saturn's ring system in 1659.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: A faint, narrow ringlet — the Huygens Ringlet — sits right at the centre of this gap, kept in place by a subtle gravitational shepherd effect.

features.name: Encke Gap
features.description: A 325-kilometre-wide gap in the outer A ring, the Encke Gap is kept open by the tiny moon Pan, which orbits within it. Pan's gravity scatters ring particles outward, creating the gap and sculpting distinctive edge waves.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pan has a distinctive equatorial ridge that makes it look like a flying saucer — material from the ring has accumulated along its equator over billions of years.

features.name: Keeler Gap
features.description: A narrow 35-kilometre gap near the outer edge of the A ring, kept open by the moonlet Daphnis. Daphnis raises spectacular wave patterns along the gap edges that ripple for thousands of kilometres.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The waves Daphnis raises along the gap edge cast shadows visible from Cassini — the undulations can reach 500 metres in height while only 35 km wide.

features.name: Colombo Gap
features.description: A gap in the inner C ring associated with a 1:0.5 resonance with Titan. Within the gap sits the Colombo Ringlet, an eccentric ringlet that does not follow a circular orbit — its centre is offset from Saturn itself.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Colombo Ringlet is one of Saturn's known eccentric ringlets — its non-circular orbit is thought to be forced by Titan's distant gravitational pull.

features.name: Maxwell Gap
features.description: A prominent 270-kilometre gap in the outer C ring, named after James Clerk Maxwell who mathematically proved in 1859 that Saturn's rings could not be solid. The gap contains the Maxwell Ringlet, another eccentric ringlet.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Maxwell proved mathematically in 1859 — before spacecraft — that if Saturn's rings were solid, they would be torn apart by tidal forces. He predicted they must be made of countless separate particles.

features.name: B Ring
features.description: The brightest and most massive of Saturn's rings, the B Ring contains most of the system's water ice. It is so densely packed that it is nearly opaque, reflecting sunlight brilliantly. Its inner structure includes mysterious spoke features — radial dark markings that rotate with Saturn's magnetic field.

details.label: Composition
details.value: Primarily water ice (>90%), with traces of silicates

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The mysterious 'spokes' — dark radial streaks that rotate with Saturn's magnetosphere rather than the ring — puzzled scientists until Cassini revealed they are charged dust grains levitated by electrostatic forces.

features.name: A Ring
features.description: The outermost of the main rings visible from Earth, the A Ring is slightly less bright than the B Ring. Its outer edge is kept sharp by a 7:6 orbital resonance with the moon Janus. The ring contains the Encke and Keeler gaps and is home to propeller-shaped disturbances caused by moonlets.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Cassini discovered hundreds of 'propellers' — two-tailed disturbances created by moonlets too small to clear a full gap but large enough to leave a gravitational wake.

features.name: F Ring
features.description: A narrow, braided, and constantly changing ring just beyond the A Ring, the F Ring is shepherded by the moons Prometheus and Pandora. Prometheus periodically dips into the ring, pulling out streamers and creating channels that give the ring its complex, kinked appearance.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Every 14.7 hours, Prometheus passes close to the F Ring and steals material from it, creating dark channels and bright clumps that can be seen forming and evolving over days.

features.name: C Ring (Crepe Ring)
features.description: The innermost of the three main rings, the C Ring is so thin and translucent it was originally called the 'Crepe Ring'. It is barely visible from Earth but shows fascinating ringlets and waves driven by resonances with Saturn's moons.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The C Ring is so transparent that stars can be seen through it from Earth — early observers called it the 'Crepe Ring' because of its gauzy, fabric-like appearance.

features.name: D Ring
features.description: The innermost known ring of Saturn, the D Ring is extremely faint and was only confirmed by Voyager 1 in 1980. It lies just above Saturn's cloud tops and is too faint to see from Earth.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Cassini detected changes in the D Ring's structure between the Voyager 1 flyby (1980) and its own arrival (2004) — the ring had shifted and developed a 30-km-scale corrugation, possibly from a comet impact.

features.name: North Polar Hexagon
features.description: One of the most striking geometric weather patterns in the solar system — a persistent hexagonal jet stream surrounding Saturn's north pole. Each side of the hexagon is about 14,500 km long, wider than Earth's diameter.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The hexagon has persisted since at least Voyager's visit in 1981 and rotates with Saturn's interior — not its upper atmosphere. The shape is likely maintained by a standing wave in the deep jet stream.

features.name: Great White Spot
features.description: Saturn periodically erupts with enormous white storms — the Great White Spots — that can encircle the entire planet. These giant thunderstorm outbreaks occur roughly every Saturnian year (29.5 Earth years), typically at northern summer.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The 2010–2011 Great White Spot was the largest in recorded history, eventually wrapping completely around Saturn. Cassini detected lightning strikes 10,000 times more powerful than Earth's.

features.name: South Polar Vortex
features.description: A permanent hurricane-like vortex at Saturn's south pole with a distinct eye and surrounding eyewall. Unlike Earth hurricanes, it doesn't drift — it stays fixed at the pole. An analogous vortex exists at the north pole, where it sits inside the hexagonal jet stream.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Unlike a tropical hurricane which is driven by warm ocean evaporation, Saturn's polar vortex is a permanent deep-atmosphere feature with no equivalent ocean beneath it.

features.name: Pan
features.description: Pan is the tiny moon that keeps Saturn's Encke Gap open. It orbits inside the A Ring and nudges nearby ring particles aside, leaving a clean lane through the ice while collecting loose material around its equator.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pan's equatorial ridge makes it look like a tiny flying saucer, probably built from ring material gathered along its orbit.

features.name: Daphnis
features.description: Daphnis is a small moonlet embedded in the Keeler Gap near the outer edge of the A Ring. Its slightly tilted orbit pulls on the gap edges and raises rippling waves that Cassini saw casting shadows across the rings.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Daphnis is nicknamed the wave maker because its gravity corrugates both edges of the narrow Keeler Gap.

features.name: Prometheus
features.description: Prometheus is the inner shepherd of Saturn's restless F Ring. As it sweeps around Saturn, it repeatedly tugs streamers of icy particles out of the ring and leaves dark channels that change from orbit to orbit.

details.label: Ring position
details.value: Inner edge of the F Ring

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Prometheus acts like a sculptor, pulling temporary braids, clumps, and channels through the F Ring every close pass.

features.name: Pandora
features.description: Pandora travels just outside the F Ring and helps define the ring's outer boundary. Together with Prometheus, it gives the F Ring its famously braided and kinked structure, although the two moons do not shepherd it in a simple steady way.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pandora's gravity is part of the reason the F Ring never looks perfectly smooth; it helps keep the ring narrow but dynamically messy.

features.name: Epimetheus
features.description: Epimetheus is one half of Saturn's remarkable co-orbital moon pair. It shares nearly the same path as Janus, and every few years the two moons gravitationally trade orbital positions instead of colliding.

details.label: Ring position
details.value: Beyond the F Ring, inside Mimas's orbit

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Epimetheus and Janus perform a rare orbital swap about every four years, passing close enough to exchange momentum but not enough to merge.

features.name: Janus
features.description: Janus is the larger partner in Saturn's co-orbital pair with Epimetheus. Its gravity helps maintain the sharp outer edge of the A Ring through orbital resonance while it shares a swapping orbit farther outside the F Ring.

details.label: Ring position
details.value: Beyond the F Ring, inside Mimas's orbit

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Janus helps hold the A Ring's outer edge in place through a 7:6 resonance, linking a small moon to one of Saturn's biggest ring boundaries.
